sections.h2: Which Georgia agency settles landlord and tenant disputes?
sections.html:
None does. The state's Landlord-Tenant Handbook says Georgia has no government agency with power to step into a rental dispute or compel either side to act. People who cannot settle a disagreement go to court, on their own or with a lawyer.

The Department of Community Affairs hosts the handbook, and since 2021 Georgia State University and the University of Georgia have edited and updated it. English and Spanish PDFs are posted. A seller weighing what to do with a tenant-occupied house, or an owner thinking about renting one out, can use it as the plain-language baseline for the points below.

sections.h2: How much security deposit can a Georgia landlord hold?
sections.html:
A landlord may not demand more than two months of rent. Owners of more than ten rental units, counting units held by a spouse or children, and owners who hire a management agent face extra duties.

  • They must put deposits into a bank escrow account used only for that purpose, or post a bond with the superior court clerk, and tell tenants in writing where the money sits.
  • They must hand over a written list of existing damage before accepting a deposit, let the tenant check it, and have both sides sign.
  • After a lease ends, they have three business days, or a reasonable time after learning the tenant left, to inspect and list damage with estimated costs.

The tenant may inspect during the first five business days after termination and should sign the list or write down what is disputed. A tenant who gave proper notice and owes nothing is entitled to the deposit back within thirty days. Ordinary wear and tear cannot be charged against it.

sections.h2: What happens to a tenant's deposit and lease when the owner sells?
sections.html:
The deposit travels with the sale. According to the handbook, the former owner either passes it to the new owner, who then answers for it, or returns it to the tenant. A tenant left without either can sue, and the handbook suggests writing to both owners first to ask about the money.

As for the lease itself, the handbook says an apartment complex that changes hands generally remains bound by existing leases, so new owners cannot raise rent or alter rules mid-term. A seller handing over an occupied rental should give the buyer the signed lease, the deposit amount and the move-in damage list.

sections.h2: How much notice ends a month-to-month tenancy in Georgia?
sections.html:
A landlord needs to give sixty days, and a tenant needs to give thirty. The handbook calls this arrangement a tenancy-at-will, and it also requires sixty days' notice before a changed rent amount takes hold.

Fixed-term leases run by their own wording, and a landlord filing for eviction must follow that wording on notice and termination.

sections.h2: Can a Georgia tenant leave a lease early?
sections.html:
Only on the lease's terms, with narrow exceptions for service members relocating on orders and tenants fleeing family violence. A tenant who abandons the unit without a lawful reason may owe the landlord money.

Early termination fees are allowed when three conditions hold: the landlord's loss is hard to estimate, both sides meant the fee to cover damages and not to punish, and the amount is a reasonable estimate. If the tenant leaves without permission, the handbook says the landlord is not required to find a new tenant and can let the unit sit empty while holding the tenant to rent through the end of the lease, unless the landlord accepts the departure.

sections.h2: What if the landlord's property is foreclosed?
sections.html:
The original landlord-tenant relationship ends, and the lender or new owner can pursue an eviction. The handbook says a tenant is not removed automatically, and a new owner may choose to set up a fresh arrangement with the tenant. An owner who wants the tenant out still has to give notice.

One trap: if a new owner has started eviction proceedings and then takes or asks for rent, a valid tenancy-at-will can result. Everyone involved should keep written notices.

sections.h2: What repairs does a Georgia landlord owe?
sections.html:
A rental must be kept safe, habitable and in good repair. The handbook breaks that down into maintaining the building structure, keeping electric, heating, cooling and plumbing working, and using ordinary care to keep the unit safe.

A lease cannot excuse those duties or declare that the landlord need not follow local laws or Georgia's deposit rules. Tenants should report problems promptly, in writing if possible and in the manner the lease requires. Problems that were obvious at move-in are usually the tenant's, unless they make the unit unsafe or uninhabitable.

Landlord retaliation for repair requests or code complaints is unlawful. Filing for eviction, reducing services or raising rent soon afterward is presumed retaliatory unless the landlord shows a lawful reason, such as unpaid rent or serious lease violations.

sections.h2: How does a Georgia eviction case unfold?
sections.html:
It begins with a demand for possession. The demand does not have to be written unless the reason is unpaid rent, and the handbook says no special words are needed. The landlord then files a dispossessory affidavit, most often in magistrate court, though state, superior and some municipal courts can hear one.

After service, the tenant has seven days to answer, and the answer should include every defense and counterclaim. Without an answer the court can order the tenant out and send the sheriff. In a nonpayment case, a tenant who pays the full alleged amount plus court costs within seven days stops the eviction, but only once in a twelve-month stretch. If the landlord will not take the money, the tenant says so in the answer, and a court finding a proper offer can require the landlord to accept payment made within three days of its ruling.

Courts may require or suggest mediation before the hearing. A mediator does not decide the case.

sections.h2: Do fair housing, lead paint and squatter rules affect a rental sale?
sections.html:
Yes. Fair housing law protects classes including race, color, religion, sex, national origin, familial status and disability, and a landlord must allow reasonable accommodations for tenants with disabilities.

Owners renting units built before 1978 must disclose known lead-based paint and hazards in the unit and common areas unless a state-certified inspector finds none. The handbook also defines a squatter as someone who never had the owner's permission to enter. The owner can swear an affidavit to have that person removed without an eviction case, and the squatter may face criminal penalties. People who stay past a lease are covered by the dispossessory steps above.

Free legal help comes from the Georgia Legal Services Program, Atlanta Legal Aid Society in Fulton, DeKalb, Cobb, Gwinnett and Clayton counties, and georgialegalaid.org.

faqs.q: Can a Georgia landlord charge a deposit of three months' rent?
faqs.a: No. The handbook says a landlord cannot require a security deposit worth more than two months of rent.

faqs.q: Does a tenant have to leave when the landlord sells the house?
faqs.a: Not automatically. The handbook says new owners are generally subject to existing leases, and a tenant-at-will is owed sixty days of notice from the landlord.

faqs.q: How long does a landlord have to return a deposit in Georgia?
faqs.a: Thirty days when the tenant gave proper notice and left owing nothing. Normal wear and tear cannot be deducted.

faqs.q: Can a tenant stop an eviction by paying what is owed?
faqs.a: Yes, in nonpayment cases, if the tenant pays the alleged rent, fees and court costs within seven days of service. The tender defense works once in any twelve-month period.

faqs.q: Who can I call for free help with a rental dispute?
faqs.a: The Georgia Legal Services Program covers most of the state, and Atlanta Legal Aid Society serves Fulton, DeKalb, Cobb, Gwinnett and Clayton counties. The handbook also points to georgialegalaid.org for self-help guides.
